doc.title: Eddie Bert interviewed by Monk Rowe, Danbury, Connecticut, November 20, 2001

title: Bebop, dancing and concerts
summary: Bebop as an evolution and the move from dance music to concerts.

story.theme_name: Playing for dancers: dance bands and the dances themselves
story.community_name: Dancing to the band: quadrilles, waltzes and dance sets

blocks.x: What did you think of the bebop era when it came in, and was it called bebop at the time or maybe that was after the fact.

Yeah I think the critics give boxes to things. It was an evolution, not a revolution. I mean it just happened. We used to go out and blow, and you’d be blowing like that, but when you come into the band you had to fit in with the band and you had to disregard a lot of that stuff. But eventually it came out with the small groups, you know, Charlie Parker and Dizzy and all them. Dizzy’s band could do that and also Billy Eckstine’s band. I mean they played that way, but not the general bands.
What happened to the audience for the music during - oh gosh, mid 50s I guess.

Well I guess it got to be concerts instead of dancing. The dancing is just starting to come back now, the last few years. But bands in the early days played for dancing. Even Duke and Basie and all them, I mean they played for dancing. But then it got to be concerts and the dances went another direction.
Do you think that was a good or bad thing?
It wasn’t good. I’d much rather play for dancing. I like to see people dancing and enjoying themselves. I mean concerts are kind of a drag.
So we’ve kind of made the music into a high art I guess.

Yeah. Right. I mean I don’t know if anybody understands that. It’s like a language. bebop, so-called bebop, that’s a language. It’s a way of — we’re talking to each other when we’re playing. That’s what it is.
